[[File:Rubus flagellaris - Dewberry.jpg|thumb|Flowers]]

'''''Rubus flagellaris''''' is a North American species of dewberry in the genus ''[[Rubus]]'', a member of the [[Rosaceae|rose family]]. It is commonly known as '''northern dewberry''' and '''common dewberry'''.<ref name=Illinois>{{cite web|url=http://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/savanna/plants/cm_dewberry.htm|work=Wildflowers of Illinois in Savannas & Thickets|title=Common Dewberry|author=Hilty, John |access-date=April 29, 2012}}</ref><ref name=USDA>{{cite web|url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=RUFL|work=Plants Database|author=Natural Resources Conservation Service|publisher=United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) | title=''Rubus flagellaris'' Willd. − northern dewberry |access-date=April 29, 2015}}</ref> It is widely distributed across the southern and eastern United States into adjacent Canada.

==Description==
''Rubus flagellaris'' has low-growing stems that range from {{convert|8|-|15|ft|m}} long, and flowering stems that can grow up to {{convert|4|ft|m}} in height. It can grow as a woody vine or low growing shrub. The young stems are green with a scattered arrangement of hairy prickles. The old stems are brown, woody and have hard [[Thorns, spines, and prickles|prickles]] in comparison to the young stem. Sometimes the tips of the young stems root into the ground and form vegetative offsets.<ref name=Illinois/><ref name=tammy>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242417161 Flora of North America, ''Rubus flagellaris'' Willdenow, 1809. Northern dewberry, ronce à flagelles ]</ref>

The species has its most active growth from mid-spring to early summer. The roots of the northern dewberry consist of a woody [[taproot]].<ref name=Illinois/><ref name=tammy/>

The plant has an alternate, [[compound leaf]] arrangement, with mostly three, but sometimes five leaflets per leaf. The [[Leaf margin|margins]] of the leaves are serrated and the leaves show a [[palmate]] venation.<ref name=dendro>{{cite web|url=https://dendro.cnre.vt.edu/dendrology/syllabus/factsheet.cfm?ID=397 | publisher=Virginia Tech Department of Forest Resources and Environmental Conservation|title=dewberry Rosaceae ''Rubus flagellaris'' Willd.|author1=Seiler, John |author2=Jensen, Edward |author3=Niemiera, Alex |author4=Peterson, John |date=2011 |access-date=April 30, 2012}}</ref> Each leaflet is ovate, approximately three inches (75 mm) long and one inch (25 mm) wide. The leaflets are green on top, but pale green on the underside.<ref name=Illinois/> One leaflet of a set is connected by a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] to the stem while the other leaflets in the set are connected to that terminal leaflet.<ref name=tammy/>

The plant produces a five-petaled white flower about one inch (25 mm) in diameter.<ref name=dendro/> The flowers exhibit a terminal inflorescence with one to five flowers per young stem.<ref name=wisplants/> The flowers are hermaphrodites and have both female and male sex organs.<ref name=pfaf>{{cite web| url=https://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Rubus+flagellaris |work=Plants for a Future|title=Rubus flagellaris - Willd.|access-date=April 30, 2012}}</ref> There are five sepals, green in appearance, [[lanceolate]] in shape. The ovaries exhibit a superior position relative to the [[sepals]] and [[petals]]. Several [[stamen]] surround a cluster of [[carpels]].<ref name=Illinois/> The flowers open during the day and close at night. 

Once the flowers of the northern dewberry are fertilized, [[drupe]]s soon grow and replace each flower.<ref name=Illinois/> The drupes are a dark-purplish color and range from ½ inch to one inch in diameter.<ref name=Illinois/><ref name=dendro/> Once the fruit has fully ripened it has a tart-sweet flavor.<ref name=Illinois/><ref name=tammy/>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Rubus flagellaris'' is native to the central and eastern United States (from [[Texas]], [[Oklahoma]], [[Kansas]], and [[Nebraska]] to the [[Gulf Coast of the United States|Gulf]] and [[East Coast of the United States|East Coast]]s and the [[Great Lakes region]]), eastern Canada ([[Ontario]], [[Quebec]], [[New Brunswick]], and [[Nova Scotia]]) and northern Mexico ([[Coahuila]], [[Hidalgo (state)|Hidalgo]], [[Nuevo León]], [[San Luis Potosí]], [[Sonora]]).<ref name=USDA/><ref name=tammy/><ref>[https://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Rubus%20flagellaris.png Biota of North America Program 2014 county distribution map]</ref>

''Rubus flagellaris'' grows on dry soils, bogs, soft soils and wooded soils.<ref name=wisplants>{{cite web|url=http://wisplants.uwsp.edu/scripts/detail.asp?SpCode=RUBFLA |work=Robert W. Freckmann Herbarium|title=Family Rosaceae ''Rubus flagellaris'' Willd|access-date=April 30, 2012}}</ref> This species is actually especially adapted to coarse textured soils (such as sandy soils), fine textured soils (such as loamy soils) and medium textured soils (such as clay-textured soils).<ref name=USDA/> ''R. flagellaris'' grows in a wide range of habitats including mesic to dry savannas and sandy savannas, abandoned fields, [[meadows]] in wooded areas, and woodland borders.<ref name=Illinois/><ref name=tammy/>

''Rubus flagellaris'' is adapted to a precipitation zone that ranges from 15 to 40 inches/year, tolerates soils ranging from 5.0 to 7.0 pH, and can survive temperatures as low as {{cvt|-23|F}}.  This species has a low tolerance to drought conditions and an intermediate shade tolerance, when compared to other species with similar growth habits in its natural regions. The plant has no salinity tolerance.<ref name=USDA/>

== Ecology ==
Many animals such as raccoons, fox squirrels, eastern chipmunks, white-footed mice, and other mammals eat the northern dewberry's fruits, and aid in the dispersal of the shrub.<ref name=Illinois/> The plant has a high tolerance to hedging from livestock or wildlife browsing.<ref name=USDA/>

The flowers, with a fragrant nectar, attract a large number of native bees. They also provide nesting materials and structures for the native bees.<ref name=wildflower>[http://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=RUFL ‘’Lary Bird Johnson Wildflower Center’’, ''Rubus flagellaris'' Willd, April 30, 2012]</ref> Some of the bee species that interact with the plant and pollinate the flowers are [[mason bee]]s (of the genus ''Osmia''), leaf-cutting bees, [[cuckoo bee]]s (of the subfamily [[Nomadinae]]), and miner bees.<ref name=Illinois/> Other insects that interact with the northern dewberry to help pollinate it are ''[[Siphonophora rubi]]'' (blackberry aphid), ''[[Metallus rubi]]'' (blackberry leafminer), ''[[Agrilus ruficollis]]'' (red-necked cane borer), and ''{{ill|Edwardsiana rosae|pl|Skoczek różany}}'' (rose leafhopper).<ref name=Illinois/>

The flowers are also a preferred source of nectar for the [[Karner blue]], an endangered species of blue [[butterfly]] found in the Midwestern U.S. and northeastern North America.<ref name=KarnerBlue>{{cite journal|doi=10.1674/0003-0031(2000)144[0001:NPSBTK]2.0.CO;2|author1=Grundel, Ralph |author2=Pavlovic, Noel B. |author3=Sulzman, Christina L |year=2000|title=Nectar plant selection by the Karner blue butterfly (Lycaeides melissa samuelis) at the Indiana Dunes National Lakeshore|journal=The American Midland Naturalist|volume=144|issue=1|pages=1–10|jstor=3083005|issn=0003-0031}}</ref>

When occasional wildfires burn down tall woody trees surrounding ''R. flagellaris'', the resulting burning has a positive effect on population growth for the species.<ref name=Illinois/> Other research has also shown that occasional wildfires are beneficial to the population's growth.<ref name=forestfire>{{cite journal| jstor=4034296 |author=Taft, John B. |journal=Castanea|volume=70|issue=4 |date=December 2005|pages=298–313 |title=Fire Effects on Structure, Composition, and Diversity in a South-Central Illinois Flatwoods Remnant| doi=10.2179/0008-7475(2005)070[0298:FEOSCA]2.0.CO;2| issn=0008-7475}}</ref>

''Rubus flagellaris'' is insect pollinated and is recorded to have been visited in northern Florida by ''[[Lasioglossum pectorale]]'', ''[[Ceratina]]'', and ''Osmia inspergens''. <ref>Ulyshen, M. D., K. Robertson, S. Horn, and C. Dixon. 2024. Characterization of the bee community and pollination network in a southeastern U.S. pine savanna. Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution 12:1403602.</ref>

==Uses==
The ripe berries are edible and can be eaten raw. They are also used to make preserves, pies, and cobblers.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://tpwmagazine.com/archive/2013/aug/ed_3_wildharvest/|title=Wild Harvest: Texas' Bounty of Native Fruits{{!}}{{!}} TPW magazine{{!}}August/September 2013|website=tpwmagazine.com|access-date=2019-03-06}}</ref>
